items.prompt: Which technique is the standard primary defense against SQL injection?

options.label: Parameterized queries
Client-side form checks
Hiding the database port
Serving pages over HTTPS

rubric: Parameterized queries (prepared statements) keep user input separate from SQL code.
HTTPS and hidden ports do not stop malicious input reaching the query.

items.prompt: What does the acronym XSS stand for?

options.label: Cross-site scripting
Extended style sheets
Cross-site sessions
Cross-server scripting

rubric: XSS is cross-site scripting.
Other options are look-alike terms that do not name a real attack.

items.prompt: Which HTTP response header lets a site declare which sources of scripts the browser may load and run?

options.label: Content-Type
Accept-Language
Cache-Control
Content-Security-Policy

rubric: Content-Security-Policy restricts the sources of scripts and other content.
Content-Type only declares the media type, and Cache-Control governs caching.

items.prompt: Which cookie attribute prevents JavaScript running in the page from reading the cookie?

options.label: Path
HttpOnly
Secure
Expires

rubric: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie.
Secure only limits the cookie to HTTPS, which is a common mix-up.

items.prompt: What does CSRF stand for?

options.label: Client-side request forwarding
Cross-site request forgery
Cross-script resource filtering
Cross-server response forgery

rubric: CSRF is cross-site request forgery.
Other options are invented phrases built from similar words.

items.prompt: Which of the following are recognized defenses against CSRF? Select all that apply.

options.label: Output encoding of user input
Salted password hashing
The SameSite cookie attribute
Anti-CSRF tokens in forms

rubric: Anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies stop forged cross-site requests.
Output encoding targets XSS and password hashing protects stored credentials.

items.prompt: A team notices that their login form sends usernames and passwords to the server over plain `http://`, so anyone on the network can read them. Which technology should they adopt to encrypt traffic between browser and server?

options.label: MD5 hashing
TLS (HTTPS)
CORS headers
Base64 encoding

rubric: TLS, used through HTTPS, encrypts data in transit.
Base64 is encoding, not encryption, and CORS controls cross-origin access.

items.prompt: Why do parameterized queries prevent SQL injection?

options.label: Input is checked by the browser first, so the server never sees bad values
Input has every quote character deleted before the query text is assembled
Input is sent separately from the query text, so it is treated only as data
Input is encrypted before the query runs, so special characters become harmless

rubric: The database fixes the query structure first, so input cannot change its meaning.
Stripping characters or browser checks can be bypassed and are not the mechanism.

items.prompt: An attacker posts a comment containing a script. The site saves it and runs it for every visitor who views the page. Which type of attack is this?

options.label: CSRF
SQL injection
Stored XSS
Reflected XSS

rubric: Payload saved on the server and served to many users is stored XSS.
Reflected XSS comes from a single request, not saved data.

items.prompt: A page inserts a user's name into HTML without encoding. A user sets their name to `<script>alert(1)</script>`. What will most likely happen when the page loads?

options.label: The name is shown on the page as plain text, tags included
The database rejects the stored name as invalid input
The browser runs the script as part of the page
The server rejects the request with a validation error

rubric: Unencoded input is parsed as HTML, so the browser executes the script.
Showing plain text would only happen if the output were encoded.

items.prompt: Why can a malicious site trigger a CSRF attack against a bank where the user is logged in?

options.label: The bank's login passwords are sent unencrypted, so the malicious site can capture them
The malicious site can read the bank's session cookie and copy it into its own requests
The bank's server cannot tell which HTTP method was used, so it accepts any request
The browser automatically attaches the bank's cookies to requests sent to the bank

rubric: Browsers add cookies automatically, so forged requests look authenticated.
The attacker does not read cookies; same-origin policy blocks that.

items.prompt: Why is validating input only in the browser not enough to secure a web app?

options.label: Browsers differ in how they run validation scripts, so checks fail unpredictably
Validation in JavaScript slows the page enough that users turn it off
Attackers can skip the browser and send requests straight to the server
Server code cannot apply the same rules that the browser form applies

rubric: Client-side checks are under the user's control and easily bypassed.
The server must validate again; speed and capability are not the issue.

items.prompt: Which of the following are examples of insecure configuration in a web application? Select all that apply.

options.label: Default admin credentials left active
Applying security patches regularly
Disabling services the app does not use
Directory listing enabled on the web server
Detailed stack traces shown to users

rubric: Default credentials, verbose errors and directory listing expose the app or its internals.
Patching and disabling unused services are hardening steps.

items.prompt: A shop's error page shows the full stack trace, including SQL table names and the server's file paths, whenever a request fails. A tester flags this as a security issue. Why is it a problem?

options.label: It lets attackers bypass parameterized queries in the database layer
It reveals internal details that help an attacker plan attacks
It slows page loads, so attackers can overload the server more easily
It breaks the browser's same-origin policy checks for the shop's pages

rubric: Verbose errors leak internals such as table names and paths, which aids attackers.
The leak is an information disclosure issue, unrelated to speed or same-origin policy.

items.prompt: Why do parameterized queries prevent SQL injection?

options.label: They limit each query to a single row so injected statements return no extra data
They strip quotes and semicolons from input before the database sees the query
They encrypt the query string so an attacker cannot read or alter its structure
They send user input separately from the SQL text, so it is treated only as data

rubric: Parameters are bound as values and never parsed as SQL syntax.
Stripping characters is a fragile filter, not the mechanism of parameterization.

items.prompt: A forum saves each comment in its database and shows it unescaped to everyone who opens the thread. A comment containing a script tag runs for every visitor. What type of XSS is this?

options.label: Stored XSS, since the payload is saved on the server and served to later visitors
Reflected XSS, since the payload is sent in the request and echoed back unescaped in the response page
DOM-based XSS, since the script is run by client-side code that writes page data into the DOM
Self-XSS, since the attacker only attacks their own browser session by pasting code into it

rubric: Payloads persisted server-side and served to other users are stored XSS.
Reflected XSS needs the victim to follow a crafted link; here no link is needed.

items.prompt: What makes cross-site request forgery (CSRF) possible against a site that uses cookie-based sessions?

options.label: Browsers attach the site's cookies to requests triggered from other sites
Session cookies are stored unencrypted in plain text on the server's disk
HTTP requests never include any header showing which page started them
Attackers can read the victim's cookies using JavaScript on their own page

rubric: Browsers attach cookies automatically, so a forged cross-site request looks authenticated.
Reading cookies cross-site is blocked by the same-origin policy; CSRF doesn't need it.

items.prompt: What does the HttpOnly flag on a session cookie do?

options.label: It forces the browser to send the cookie only over encrypted HTTPS connections, never over plain HTTP
It stops page JavaScript from reading the cookie, so XSS cannot steal it directly
It prevents the browser from sending the cookie on requests that start from other sites
It makes the cookie expire when the browser tab is closed by the user

rubric: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie.
Sending only over HTTPS is Secure; cross-site restriction is SameSite.

items.prompt: Why is validating a form only with client-side JavaScript not enough to protect a web application?

options.label: Client-side checks cannot compare values against any regular expression
Browsers disable validation scripts when the page is loaded over HTTPS
JavaScript validation is too slow to catch malicious values in time
An attacker can send requests directly to the server and skip the browser code

rubric: Attackers control the client and can bypass its checks, so the server must validate.
The other options invent technical limits that don't exist.

items.prompt: Which of the following are examples of insecure configuration? Select all that apply.

options.label: The default admin password of a framework console is left unchanged
Directory listing is enabled on a folder holding uploaded files
The site sends an HSTS header telling browsers to use HTTPS only
Error pages show full stack traces and database details to visitors

rubric: Default credentials, verbose errors and open directory listings expose the app.
HSTS is a hardening setting, not a misconfiguration.

items.prompt: A search page shows the text 'You searched for: ' followed by the q parameter from the URL, without escaping it. A tester opens a link with q set to a script tag and sees the script run. Nothing is stored on the server. What best classifies this flaw?

options.label: Reflected XSS, because the input in the request is echoed straight into the response
SQL injection, because the URL parameter is placed into a query that builds the page
CSRF, because the link makes the browser send a request the user never intended to make
Stored XSS, because the script stays on the server and runs for every later visitor

rubric: Input echoed immediately into the response without escaping is reflected XSS.
Stored XSS needs persistence; CSRF forges actions rather than running script.

items.prompt: A Node app builds a query with `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"`. Which replacement removes the injection risk?

options.label: `db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", [name])`
`db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name.slice(0, 20) + "'")`
`db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name.toLowerCase() + "'")`
`db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name.trim() + "'")`

rubric: A placeholder binds name as data.
Trimming, lowercasing or truncating still concatenates input into the SQL.

items.prompt: A page inserts a user's bio into the HTML body. The bio is `Hi`. Which output shows the text literally instead of rendering bold when HTML-encoded?

options.label: `<b>Hi</b>`
`%3Cb%3EHi%3C%2Fb%3E`

rubric: HTML-encoding turns angle brackets into entities so the browser shows them as text.
URL and JavaScript escapes are for other contexts and won't encode correctly in an HTML body.

items.prompt: You must protect a cookie-authenticated `POST /change-email` form against CSRF. Which change do you make?

options.label: Serve the form only over HTTPS and extend the session cookie lifetime so users stay signed in
Put a random per-session token in the form and reject requests missing it
Check that the Content-Length header on each incoming request is within the expected limits
Hide the form's submit button until a script has verified that the user's session is valid

rubric: A secret token an attacker's page cannot know proves the request came from your form.
HTTPS and cookie lifetime don't stop the browser attaching cookies to forged requests.

items.prompt: Which Set-Cookie header correctly hardens a session cookie against script access, plaintext transport and most cross-site sends?

options.label: `Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; SameSite=None; Domain=.com`
`Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`
`Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Secure; SameSite=None; Path=/`
`Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Secure; Path=/; Max-Age=999999`

rubric: HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax cover the three goals.
Other options omit HttpOnly or Secure, or allow cross-site sending with SameSite=None.

items.prompt: A script shows a user comment with `box.innerHTML = comment;`. Which line displays it safely as plain text?

options.label: `box.innerHTML = comment.toLowerCase();`
`box.textContent = comment;`
`box.innerHTML = comment.trim();`
`box.outerHTML = comment;`

rubric: textContent treats the value as text, never as markup.
Trimming, lowercasing or outerHTML still parse markup and can run event handlers.

items.prompt: A bank app uses cookie sessions and has a state-changing `POST /transfer` endpoint. Which changes help stop CSRF against it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Change the endpoint to `GET /transfer` so it is easier to log
Set SameSite=Lax or Strict on the session cookie
Validate a per-session anti-CSRF token on each POST
Validate the amount field with JavaScript before the form submits

rubric: SameSite cookies and anti-CSRF tokens both stop forged cross-site requests.
GET for state changes worsens CSRF, and client-side validation doesn't affect forged requests.

items.prompt: A product list endpoint builds `"SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY " + req.query.sort`. A developer tries a placeholder for the column name, but the database rejects it. The sort values the UI uses are price, name and rating. What is the best fix?

options.label: Escape single quotes and backslashes in the sort value, then keep concatenating it into the query
Run the query as a lower-privilege read-only database user and keep the current concatenation
Accept the sort value only if it is price, name or rating, then use it in the query
Wrap the sort value in a parameter placeholder and cast it to a string before running the query

rubric: Identifiers can't be bound as parameters, so an allow-list of known columns is the standard defense.
Quote escaping doesn't help in an unquoted position, and privilege reduction doesn't remove the injection.

items.prompt: A search feature must find items whose name contains the user's term. Which database call is safe against SQL injection?

options.label: `db.query("SELECT * FROM items WHERE name LIKE '%" + esc(term) + "%'")` where `esc` doubles single quotes
`db.query("SELECT * FROM items WHERE name LIKE '%?%'", [term])`
`db.query("SELECT * FROM items WHERE name LIKE ?", ["%" + term + "%"])`
`db.query("SELECT * FROM items WHERE name LIKE '%" + term.replace(/;/g, "") + "%'")`

rubric: The wildcards are added to the bound value, so the term is always sent as data, never as SQL.
A placeholder inside quotes is a literal question mark, and hand-rolled escaping or stripping characters is incomplete.

items.prompt: A page renders `<input value="USER">`, where USER is text a visitor typed earlier. Which defense is correct for this exact output context?

options.label: Escape the value as a JavaScript string, because attribute values are evaluated as script by browsers
URL-encode the value with `encodeURIComponent` so special characters cannot be parsed by the browser
Remove only angle brackets from the value, because an attribute cannot contain tags that run
HTML-encode the value, including double quotes, so it cannot close the attribute or add new ones

rubric: In a quoted attribute the attacker must break out with a quote, so HTML attribute encoding of quotes is the matching defense.
Stripping brackets or using URL or JS encoding targets a different context and leaves attribute injection like `" onfocus=...` possible.

items.prompt: Which `Set-Cookie` attributes best protect a session cookie on an HTTPS site from script access and from being sent on most cross-site requests?

options.label: `Secure; Path=/; Max-Age=86400`
`Secure; SameSite=None; Path=/`
`HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`
`HttpOnly; Domain=.example.com; SameSite=None`

rubric: HttpOnly blocks script reads, Secure limits to HTTPS, and Lax withholds the cookie from most cross-site subrequests.
SameSite=None sends the cookie cross-site and no HttpOnly leaves it readable by injected script.

items.prompt: You must protect a state-changing `POST /settings` form from CSRF in a session-cookie app. Which server-side check is correct?

options.label: Confirm the body is URL-encoded form data, since attackers cannot forge that format from another site
Confirm the session cookie is present and valid, since browsers only send it from the user's own pages
Require a secret value stored in a cookie, since the browser attaches that cookie to every request automatically
Compare an unpredictable per-session token from a hidden form field with the server-side copy, since a cross-site page cannot read it

rubric: The attacker's page cannot read the token, so a matching token proves the request came from the app's own form.
Cookies are attached automatically to forged requests, and cross-site forms can send URL-encoded bodies.

items.prompt: A login page redirects to the URL in `?next=` after sign-in. To prevent an open redirect to phishing sites, which fix should you apply?

options.label: Reject values that do not start with `https://`, since that ensures an encrypted connection to our site
Remove the substring `http://` from the value once, then redirect to whatever remains
Accept only values matching a server-side allowlist of internal paths, else redirect to a default page
URL-encode the value before placing it in the `Location` header so it cannot be parsed as another site

rubric: An allowlist of internal destinations guarantees the redirect stays on the site.
Prefix checks, single-pass stripping and encoding all still permit external hosts such as `https://evil.example`.

items.prompt: Which changes harden the configuration of a production web application? Select all that apply.

options.label: Keep directory listing enabled so support staff can find uploaded files quickly
Return generic error pages to users and keep stack traces in server-side logs only
Send a `Content-Security-Policy` that limits `script-src` to the app's own origin and omits `unsafe-inline`
Send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with credentials so every client works
Send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` so browsers respect the declared content types

rubric: CSP, nosniff and generic errors reduce script injection, content sniffing and information leakage.
Wildcard CORS with credentials and directory listing expose data rather than harden the app.

items.prompt: A report page lets users pick a sort column from a dropdown. The server builds `"SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY " + request.sort`. The team already uses placeholders for values elsewhere. Which fix is appropriate for this clause?

options.label: Map the requested value to a fixed allowlist of column names and append only the matched name
Bind the sort value as a parameter by writing `ORDER BY ?` and passing the request value
Pass the sort string as an argument to a stored procedure that concatenates it inside the database
Escape single quotes in the value, since column names in ORDER BY are not wrapped in quotes

rubric: Identifiers cannot be bound as parameters, so only known column names from an allowlist should reach the SQL text.
Binding yields a constant expression, and escaping quotes or moving concatenation into a procedure still allows injection.

items.prompt: A comment form deletes the text `

options.label: The comment is saved in the database, so storing user text at all is what creates the vulnerability
The filter is case-sensitive, so the real fix is to also strip `<SCRIPT>` and similar variants
The defense is an input blacklist rather than encoding output for the HTML context where data is rendered
The `img` tag loads an external resource, so blocking image tags in comments removes the underlying cause

rubric: Blacklists miss countless payloads; encoding on output for the right context neutralises any markup.
Adding variants or blocking one tag just moves to the next payload, and storing text is not itself the flaw.

items.prompt: An app sets its session cookie `SameSite=Lax`. A link on an attacker's site sends the victim to `https://bank.example/transfer?to=x&amt=100`, and the transfer executes. Why did Lax not prevent it?

options.label: Lax cookies are still sent on top-level GET navigations, and this app changes state on a GET request
SameSite is ignored over HTTPS unless the cookie also carries the `HttpOnly` attribute in the header
Lax only restricts cookies on same-site requests, so every cross-site request carries the cookie anyway
Browsers send Lax cookies on any cross-site request started by a link, form post, image or script

rubric: Lax allows cookies on top-level navigations using safe methods, so state changes must never happen on GET.
The distractors misstate Lax as sending cookies on all cross-site requests, or as depending on HttpOnly.

items.prompt: `GET /invoices/1042` returns any invoice to any logged-in user who guesses the ID. Authentication itself works correctly. What is the root flaw?

options.label: GET is the wrong HTTP method; a POST lookup would block unauthorized reads
No rate limiting, so attackers can enumerate invoice IDs freely
The server never checks that the invoice belongs to the requesting user
Invoice IDs are sequential and guessable; random IDs would fully fix it

rubric: Access to an object must be authorised per object; authentication only proves identity.
Random IDs, POST and rate limits only obscure or slow the attack while the missing ownership check remains.

items.prompt: An API echoes the request's `Origin` header into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and also sends `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. What does this enable?

options.label: Any website a logged-in user visits can read that user's authenticated API responses
Attackers can send forged requests but cannot read responses, since browsers block cross-origin reads
Attackers can downgrade the connection to HTTP, since the origin check ignores the URL scheme
Attackers can inject SQL through the Origin header, since the server copies its value into queries

rubric: Reflecting any origin with credentials lets attacker pages read private data using the victim's cookies.
The distractors describe CSRF-only, SQL injection or downgrade attacks that this header pairing does not cause.

items.prompt: An attacker plants a known session ID in a victim's browser through a crafted link. The victim then logs in, and the attacker uses that same ID to act as the victim. Which step is faulty?

options.label: The session ID is not regenerated at login, so the ID the attacker knows becomes an authenticated one
The login form is served over HTTP, so the attacker sniffed the password and then created a session
The session ID is too short, so the attacker got it by brute force before the victim signed in
The cookie lacks `HttpOnly`, so injected script read the ID after the victim had authenticated

rubric: Issuing a fresh ID on privilege change prevents a pre-planted ID from gaining authenticated access.
The distractors describe guessing, script theft or sniffing, none of which the scenario involves.

items.prompt: An app uses parameterized queries for user input, yet a SQL injection is confirmed. Which situations could explain it? Select all that apply.

options.label: A bound parameter contains a single quote character that the driver then passes through
The prepared statement is reused across several requests on a pooled connection
A stored procedure builds a dynamic SQL string by concatenating its argument
A value saved safely earlier is read back and concatenated into a later query
The sort direction from the request is concatenated into the `ORDER BY` clause

rubric: Injection survives wherever untrusted text still reaches SQL text: identifiers, dynamic SQL in procedures, and second-order use.
Quotes in bound values and statement reuse are handled as data and do not cause injection.

items.prompt: A profile page renders `My website`. The app HTML-encodes USER_URL, yet a user sets it to `javascript:alert(document.cookie)` and the script runs on click. What is the best diagnosis and fix?

options.label: Encoding was applied too early, so encode twice and the colon will become an entity
The cookie lacks `HttpOnly`, so setting that flag removes the vulnerability entirely
The double quotes were not encoded, so the payload broke out of the attribute and added a handler
HTML encoding does not cover URL context; validate that the scheme is http or https before output

rubric: The payload needs no quotes or brackets; the dangerous part is the URL scheme, which only a scheme allowlist stops.
Double encoding and HttpOnly do not stop script execution, and no attribute breakout occurs here.

items.prompt: A comment filter removes `

options.label: The regex is case sensitive, so adding a case-insensitive flag would fully close the hole in the filter
The filter targets one known tag instead of encoding output for the HTML context where the data is rendered
Image tags are always unsafe, so the filter should drop every tag that can load an external resource
The filter runs on the server, when it should run in the browser so that it sees the final rendered DOM

rubric: Blacklist filtering on input misses other script vectors; context-aware output encoding addresses the actual cause.
Distractors treat the problem as a regex detail or a tag-specific issue, which leaves other event-handler vectors open.

items.prompt: A site sets its session cookie with `SameSite=Lax`. It also has an endpoint `GET /account/delete?confirm=1` that deletes the logged-in account. Why can an attacker's page still trigger the deletion?

options.label: Lax cookies are sent on cross-site top-level GET navigations, so a link or redirect carries the session
Lax is ignored by browsers unless the cookie also carries the `Secure` flag in the response header, which this site's cookie lacks
Lax applies only to POST requests, so every GET request is sent with cookies regardless of its origin
Lax cookies are blocked on all cross-site requests, so the attacker must be using an XSS flaw instead

rubric: Lax still sends cookies on top-level cross-site GET navigations, so state-changing GET endpoints stay CSRF-able.
Distractors misstate what Lax blocks or assume an unrelated flaw such as XSS.

items.prompt: A search endpoint binds the filter value as a parameter, but builds the clause `ORDER BY ` + `req.query.sort` by string concatenation. A tester injects SQL through `sort`. Why did parameter binding not help here?

options.label: ORDER BY is evaluated before WHERE, so the bound values are not yet substituted when it is parsed
Bound parameters are escaped by the client library, which fails on strings that contain sort keywords
Placeholders bind values only, not identifiers or keywords, so concatenated text is parsed as code
Placeholders are applied only to the first clause of a statement, so later clauses are left unescaped

rubric: Parameter binding covers literal values; column names and keywords must be allowlisted instead.
Distractors invent clause-ordering or escaping explanations that are not how prepared statements work.

items.prompt: Logs show an external client calling `/preview?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` on a thumbnail service, and the response contains cloud instance metadata. Which weakness does this reveal?

options.label: An open redirect, because the endpoint sends users to a URL that the attacker chooses to supply
XML external entity processing, because the endpoint resolves an external resource named in the input
Cross-site request forgery, because the endpoint performs an action without any anti-forgery token present
Server-side request forgery, because the server fetches user-chosen URLs from inside the trusted network

rubric: The server itself makes the request to an internal address chosen by the attacker, which is SSRF.
Distractors name other vulnerabilities that involve URLs or external references but do not match the server-side fetch.

items.prompt: An API verifies tokens with `jwt.verify(token, rsaPublicKey)` and lets the token header choose the algorithm. An attacker signs a token with HS256 using the RSA public key as the secret, and it is accepted. What went wrong?

options.label: The public key was too short, so the attacker could factor it and forge RSA signatures offline
HS256 tokens are always accepted by JWT libraries once any valid RSA token has been issued earlier
The token lacked an expiry claim, so signatures remained valid and could be replayed indefinitely
The library let the untrusted header pick HMAC, so the public key was used as a shared secret

rubric: This is algorithm confusion: the verifier must fix the expected algorithm rather than trust the header.
Distractors blame key size, expiry or library behaviour, none of which explain acceptance of a forged HMAC token.

items.prompt: A tester steals session cookies by exploiting an XSS flaw. Which findings made the impact of the XSS worse, without being its cause? Select all that apply.

options.label: Sessions never expire and are not bound to the client, so a stolen cookie works from any machine
The session cookie has the `Secure` flag, so it travels only over HTTPS
The session cookie has no `HttpOnly` flag, so page scripts can read it
Passwords are hashed with a per-user salt before they are stored

rubric: A readable cookie and a CSP that permits inline scripts both let the injected code steal the session.
The Secure flag and salted hashing are not factors in cookie theft through XSS.

items.prompt: A password reset email builds its link from the incoming `Host` header. An attacker requests a reset for a victim's account with `Host: evil.example`. The victim receives a genuine email whose link points to evil.example with a valid token, and clicking it sends the token to the attacker. What is the root cause?

options.label: The reset token is too short and predictable, so the attacker can guess it once they see the email format and then build the link themselves
The app trusts a client-controlled header to build absolute URLs instead of a configured canonical host
The email is sent over unencrypted SMTP, so the attacker can rewrite the link while the message is in transit between servers
The reset endpoint lacks rate limiting, so the attacker can request unlimited reset emails for any account and eventually intercept one

rubric: Host header injection: the link is built from attacker-controlled input instead of a fixed configured host.
Distractors point to real weaknesses that are not what let the attacker redirect the token here.

items.prompt: A forum lets users post comments with bold text, lists and links. Criteria: formatting must be kept, and protection must hold even if developers add new templates later. Which approach best meets them?

options.label: Escape all HTML on output, so users' tags show as visible text and no markup ever runs in a page
Strip `<script>` tags and `on*` attributes with regexes on input, which blocks the usual script vectors
Validate the comment in client-side JavaScript before submission, so malformed markup rarely arrives
Sanitize at render time with a maintained allowlist sanitizer, and add a CSP as a second layer of defense

rubric: An allowlist sanitizer keeps formatting and a CSP backs it up; neither depends on each template being written correctly.
Escaping everything loses formatting, regex stripping is bypassable, and client-side checks can be skipped by attackers.

items.prompt: A cookie-authenticated app has state-changing POST endpoints. Criteria: protection must hold in browsers with uneven SameSite support, and one misconfiguration must not expose every user. Which design is best?

options.label: Rely on `SameSite=Strict` alone, since modern browsers enforce it and extra tokens only add complexity
Require a JSON content type on POSTs, since cross-site forms cannot send it without a CORS preflight
Use `SameSite=Lax` cookies plus a per-session anti-CSRF token checked on every state-changing request
Accept requests only when a `Referer` header is present, since attackers cannot forge that header

rubric: Layering SameSite with a verified token gives defense in depth that survives gaps in either control.
The other options depend on a single control, a header that may be stripped, or a content-type quirk.

items.prompt: A scan of a public retail site returns four findings. Criteria: fix first the issue giving the greatest exposure of customer data for the least attacker effort. Which should be fixed first?

options.label: Stored XSS in product reviews that runs in other shoppers' browsers but cannot read the HttpOnly session cookie
Self-XSS that works only if a user pastes a payload into their own profile field
A missing CSRF token on the logged-in newsletter preferences form, which needs a victim to visit a hostile page
Unauthenticated SQL injection in the product search endpoint that concatenates input into its query

rubric: Unauthenticated injection is remotely exploitable with low effort and exposes the database, so it ranks highest.
The other findings are low impact or need unusual victim action.

items.prompt: A team proposes to prevent SQL injection with a custom function that doubles single quotes in every input before it is concatenated into queries. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: It fails because databases strip doubled quotes, so inputs would have to be wrapped in double quotes instead
It misses numeric and identifier positions and depends on encoding, while parameterized queries keep data out of code
It is adequate when paired with a maximum input length, since short inputs cannot carry a working payload at all
It is sound for string inputs, and the only real drawback is slower execution compared with prepared statements at scale

rubric: Quote doubling does not cover non-string contexts or character-set tricks; parameterization separates code from data structurally.
Distractors treat the approach as basically safe or misdescribe how databases treat escaped quotes.

items.prompt: Users upload avatar images. Criteria: block stored XSS and server-side code execution, and keep serving cheap. Which design is best?

options.label: Scan filenames for `.php` and `.js` strings, then store files in the web root so a CDN can serve them
Check the first bytes of each upload for a valid PNG or JPEG signature, then store it under its original name in the web root so a CDN can serve it
Re-encode images server-side, store under random names outside the web root, and serve with `nosniff` from a cookieless domain
Accept files whose extension is `.png` or `.jpg` and keep them in the web root under their original names

rubric: Re-encoding, random names, non-executable storage and a separate cookieless origin address both XSS and code execution.
Extension, header and filename checks are all attacker-controlled and easy to bypass.

items.prompt: An API authenticates users with cookies. Judge which CORS configurations are unsafe for it. Select all that apply.

options.label: It uses an exact allowlist of two first-party origins with credentials allowed
It sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on a public endpoint that returns no user data
It reflects any request `Origin` in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and sends `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`
It allows `Origin: null` with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`

rubric: Reflecting arbitrary origins or trusting null with credentials lets hostile pages read authenticated responses.
An exact allowlist and a wildcard on public, credential-free data do not expose user data.

items.prompt: A team builds a single-page app that embeds several third-party analytics scripts and displays user-generated content. They must choose how to hold the session credential. Criteria: limit damage if a script is injected, and keep CSRF manageable. Which choice is best?

options.label: Store the JWT in `localStorage`, since it is never sent automatically and so is immune to CSRF, making it the safest browser storage
Store the JWT in `sessionStorage`, since it clears on tab close and so cannot be read by injected scripts
Use an opaque session ID in an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax` cookie, plus CSRF tokens on state changes
Keep the JWT in a JavaScript variable and a non-HttpOnly cookie copy, so either can restore the session

rubric: An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by injected scripts, and SameSite plus tokens keeps CSRF under control.
Web storage and script-readable cookies expose the credential to any injected or third-party script.

items.prompt: A forum must let users post limited HTML (bold, links, lists). Judged on stopping stored XSS while keeping the feature, which approach is best?

options.label: HTML-encode all input before saving, which neutralizes markup in the output contexts where the post is later shown
Sanitize with a maintained allowlist library at render time, and add a CSP as a second layer
Strip <script> tags with a regex on input, since script tags are the main route for HTML to run code
Set the session cookie to HttpOnly, which blocks injected markup from running in the user's browser

rubric: Allowlist sanitization at output plus CSP gives layered defense while preserving allowed HTML.
Regex blacklists are bypassed by event handlers and encodings; input encoding is context-blind; HttpOnly only limits cookie theft.

items.prompt: A team claims SameSite=Lax on the session cookie makes CSRF tokens unnecessary. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: Lax blocks every cross-site navigation including links, so it breaks sign-in and should be None
Lax only mitigates XSS, so it has no effect on whether cookies accompany cross-site requests
Lax is ignored by modern browsers, so cookies are still sent on every cross-site request
Lax still sends cookies on top-level GET navigations, so state-changing GETs remain exploitable

rubric: Lax permits cookies on top-level GET navigations, so unsafe GET handlers remain CSRF-able.
Other options misstate what Lax does or confuse it with XSS defenses.

items.prompt: Which CORS configuration on an authenticated API poses the greatest risk?

options.label: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on a public endpoint that returns open data and needs no cookies or login
Allowing only GET and POST from one vetted partner origin, with credentials enabled for that origin
Reflecting any request Origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin while also sending Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Omitting Access-Control-Max-Age, so browsers repeat preflight requests more often than strictly needed

rubric: Reflecting arbitrary origins with credentials lets any site read authenticated responses.
Wildcard on public data and a vetted origin are acceptable; missing Max-Age is only a performance matter.

items.prompt: A SPA is served from the same site as its API. Criteria: limit damage from XSS token theft, and accept extra CSRF work. Which session storage is best?

options.label: Store a JWT in localStorage, since scripts need it for headers and CSRF then cannot occur at all
Store the JWT in sessionStorage, which clears on tab close so injected scripts cannot read it at all
Store the JWT in a JavaScript-readable cookie so the page and server can both read it easily
Use an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite session cookie plus CSRF protection on state-changing requests

rubric: HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by injected script, and CSRF defenses address the cookie trade-off.
Web storage and script-readable cookies are all exposed to XSS theft.

items.prompt: A report endpoint takes a sort column name from the query string and places it in ORDER BY. Which defense is most robust?

options.label: Escape single quotes in the value, since identifiers are only injected through quote characters
Bind the column name as a prepared-statement parameter, since parameters protect any SQL position
Remove semicolons and comment markers from the input before concatenating it into the query
Map the input to a fixed allowlist of known column names and use only the mapped value

rubric: Identifiers cannot be bound as parameters, so an allowlist mapping is the reliable control.
Escaping quotes or stripping characters is a blacklist approach that misses unquoted identifier injection.

items.prompt: A site uses the CSP `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://cdn.example.com`. Which criticisms of this policy are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: The policy is strong because the CDN is served over HTTPS, which prevents script injection
Allowlisting a shared CDN host can enable bypass through JSONP endpoints or script gadgets hosted there
'self' permits scripts from any subdomain of the site's registered domain
'unsafe-inline' lets an injected inline script or event handler run, undermining XSS protection
The policy blocks all inline event handlers, which will break many legacy pages

rubric: Both unsafe-inline and broad host allowlists are well-known CSP weaknesses.
The other options misstate what 'self' and 'unsafe-inline' do, or confuse HTTPS with injection protection.

items.prompt: An image-import feature fetches a user-supplied URL. The team blocks hosts equal to 'localhost' or '127.0.0.1'. A pentester reaches the cloud metadata address 169.254.169.254 using an attacker-owned hostname whose DNS record points to it. Which improvement best addresses the root cause?

options.label: Validate the URL with a stricter regex at submit time and trust the stored value whenever it is fetched later
Resolve the hostname, check the resulting IP against allowed public ranges, then connect to that validated IP without following redirects
Require HTTPS URLs only, since internal metadata services do not accept TLS connections from the server, and reject any plain HTTP URL
Extend the string blocklist with 0.0.0.0, [::1] and 169.254.169.254 and the decimal and hex forms of each, so every known internal address is covered

rubric: SSRF defenses must check the resolved IP and pin the connection, and handle redirects, rather than match host strings.
String blocklists and submit-time regexes are bypassed by DNS and alternate encodings.

items.prompt: Password reset constraints: links must be single-use, expire quickly, resist guessing, and not be usable if the database leaks. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: Email a link with a sequential reset ID plus a hash of the user's email, expiring in 15 minutes
Email a link with a random 128-bit token, store only its hash with an expiry, and invalidate it on first use
Email a link with a random 128-bit token, stored in plaintext for fast lookup, expiring in 15 minutes and deleted on first use
Email a link with base64 of user ID and timestamp, valid 24 hours, reusable until the password changes

rubric: Hashing the stored random token protects against DB leaks while expiry and single use limit replay.
Plaintext storage fails the leak constraint; predictable or reusable tokens fail guessing and single-use.

items.prompt: Avatar upload constraints: files must never execute as code on the app's origin, SVG-borne script must not run with the app's cookies, and filenames must not permit path traversal. Which design meets all three?

options.label: Generate random server-side names, re-encode images to raster, and serve from a separate cookieless domain with nosniff
Keep the original filename, check the extension is .png or .jpg, and store the files in the web root for fast serving
Strip '../' from filenames, allow SVG for image quality, and serve from the app domain using an inline Content-Disposition
Trust the Content-Type header sent by the browser, then store under the user-supplied name in a private folder

rubric: Random names, re-encoding and a cookieless separate origin address traversal, script execution and cookie exposure.
Extension or header checks and naive stripping are bypassable and leave uploads on the app origin.

items.prompt: A site loads many third-party scripts that load further scripts dynamically. Constraints: no host allowlists (bypass risk), block injected inline scripts, block plugin content and injected base tags. Which CSP fits?

options.label: script-src 'sha256-<one hash>' 'self'; object-src 'self'; base-uri 'self'; require-trusted-types-for 'script'
script-src https://a.example https://b.example 'unsafe-eval'; default-src *
script-src 'nonce-{random per response}' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'
script-src 'self' https: 'unsafe-inline'; object-src 'self'; base-uri 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'

rubric: A per-response nonce with strict-dynamic trusts dynamically loaded scripts without allowlists, and object-src/base-uri none close the other gaps.
Other policies keep unsafe-inline, host allowlists or permissive object and base settings.

items.prompt: A cookie-session JSON API is called by a first-party SPA on a sibling subdomain. Constraints: no server-side token storage, and defence against both cross-site and sibling-subdomain attackers who can set cookies. Which design fits?

options.label: Naive double-submit: set a random cookie and require its value in a header, with no signing or session binding
Set SameSite=None on the session cookie so the browser can distinguish first-party requests
Rely on requiring Content-Type: application/json, since cross-site HTML forms cannot send that type
Send an HMAC-signed token bound to the session ID, require it in a header, and also verify the Origin header

rubric: A signed, session-bound token is stateless and resists cookie injection from sibling subdomains; Origin adds a second check.
Naive double-submit is defeated by cookie injection; content-type reliance and SameSite=None do not stop CSRF.

items.prompt: A SPA login uses the authorization code flow with exact redirect_uri matching over HTTPS. A reviewer says two protections are missing, against login CSRF and against interception of authorization codes. Which additions complete the design?

options.label: A nonce in the URL fragment, plus wildcard redirect_uri support for subpaths
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, plus encryption of the authorization code in the query string
A state value bound to the user's session, plus PKCE with a code verifier
A client secret embedded in the SPA bundle, plus a longer-lived access token

rubric: State binds the response to the initiating session and PKCE binds the code to the client that requested it.
Embedded secrets are public in SPAs, and wildcard redirects weaken matching.

items.prompt: A banking page must not be embeddable by other sites, and an attacker who plants a known session ID before login must gain no access after the victim logs in. Which controls together satisfy this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Send CSP frame-ancestors 'none' on the page
Rely on a JavaScript frame-busting check as the only framing protection
Accept the session ID from a URL parameter for users with cookies disabled
Issue a new session ID when the user authenticates
Send X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block on all responses

rubric: frame-ancestors blocks framing, and regenerating the session ID at login defeats session fixation.
Frame-busting scripts are bypassable, URL session IDs enable fixation, and X-XSS-Protection is unrelated.

items.prompt: A multi-tenant invoicing API exposes GET /invoices/{id} with sequential IDs. A review found users reading other tenants' invoices by editing the ID. The fix must cover every current and future endpoint, must not rely on the client, and must not depend on secret IDs. Which design meets these constraints?

options.label: Add rate limiting and alerts on sequential ID enumeration, so repeated guessing is blocked or flagged quickly
Replace sequential IDs with random UUIDs and leave the handlers unchanged, since attackers cannot guess them
Scope every data-access query by the authenticated tenant in a shared layer, deny by default, and test per endpoint
Hide other tenants' invoices in the UI and check the user's role at the route level for each endpoint

rubric: Centralised tenant-scoped object-level authorization enforced server-side covers all endpoints without relying on ID secrecy.
UUIDs, UI hiding, route role checks and rate limits all leave object-level authorization gaps.
